title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At a camp near Forres a bleeding Sergeant tells Duncan how 'brave Macbeth' cut the rebel Macdonwald open 'from the nave to the chaps' and, with Banquo, fought on against a fresh Norwegian attack. Ross reports the treachery of the Thane of Cawdor and the victory over Norway. Duncan orders Cawdor's execution and gives his title to Macbeth.

context.history: Thanes were Scottish nobles holding land from the king. Rebellion (Macdonwald) and treason by a trusted noble (Cawdor) were real fears; the 1605 Gunpowder Plot was fresh in memory.

significance: We hear of Macbeth before we see him: a loyal, almost superhuman killer. The scene's dramatic irony is that the title of a traitor passes to the next traitor.
discussionQuestions: Is someone who is very good at violence a hero? When does courage become something else?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with guilt and conscience?

satQuestions.passage:
Doubtful it stood;
As two spent swimmers, that do cling together
And choke their art. The merciless Macdonwald—
Worthy to be a rebel, for to that
The multiplying villainies of nature
Do swarm upon him—from the western isles
Of kerns and gallowglasses is supplied;
And fortune, on his damned quarrel smiling,
Show’d like a rebel’s whore: but all’s too weak:
For brave Macbeth—well he deserves that name—
Disdaining fortune, with his brandish’d steel,
Which smoked with bloody execution,
Like valour’s minion carved out his passage
Till he faced the slave;
Which ne’er shook hands, nor bade farewell to him,
Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chaps,
And fix’d his head upon our battlements.

anchorPassages.text:
From Fife, great king;
Where the Norweyan banners flout the sky
And fan our people cold. Norway himself,
With terrible numbers,
Assisted by that most disloyal traitor
The thane of Cawdor, began a dismal conflict;
Till that Bellona’s bridegroom, lapp’d in proof,
Confronted him with self-comparisons,
Point against point rebellious, arm ’gainst arm,
Curbing his lavish spirit: and, to conclude,
The victory fell on us.
Great happiness!
That now
Sweno, the Norways’ king, craves composition;
Nor would we deign him burial of his men
Till he disbursed at Saint Colme’s inch
Ten thousand dollars to our general use.
No more that thane of Cawdor shall deceive
Our bosom interest: go pronounce his present death,
And with his former title greet Macbeth.
I’ll see it done.
What he hath lost noble Macbeth hath won.

segments.script: Today's words: disbursed — paid out (money); furbish — to polish and make (weapons) ready again; overcharged — loaded with too much powder; here, packed with a double charge; cannons — large guns that fire heavy shot; vantage — an opportunity or advantage. “disbursed”: Origin of “disburse”: Old French desbourser. “overcharged”: Origin of “overcharge”: an English formation from over- + charge.

segments.script: Thanes were Scottish nobles holding land from the king. Rebellion (Macdonwald) and treason by a trusted noble (Cawdor) were real fears; the 1605 Gunpowder Plot was fresh in memory. We hear of Macbeth before we see him: a loyal, almost superhuman killer. The scene's dramatic irony is that the title of a traitor passes to the next traitor. Characterization: The bleeding Sergeant's report presents Macbeth as a ferocious hero who "unseam'd" a rebel "from the nave to the chaps." Irony: Duncan gives the traitor Cawdor's title to Macbeth, the next traitor. Imagery: Blood, already: the Sergeant's wounds and Macbeth's sword "which smoked with bloody execution." Watch for kingship and order: Rightful kingship is tied to natural order; watch how disorder in the state shows up in nature.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “For brave Macbeth—well he deserves that name” slowly and put it in my own words: The wounded Sergeant tells Duncan that brave Macbeth well deserves that name for how he fought. Next, craft. I notice the interruption of his own sentence with a dash, as if he must stop to praise Macbeth. The strongest word is “brave”: it is the reputation Macbeth begins with, which makes his fall greater. Then, effect. How does the Sergeant present Macbeth to Duncan? My answer: The Sergeant presents Macbeth to Duncan as a fearless, loyal warrior who carved his way through the rebels; the praise sets up the tragedy, since his courage in battle will become ruthless ambition.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about Macbeth's reputation as a warrior? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act I, Scene II develops the idea of Macbeth's reputation as a warrior. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The play first presents Macbeth's violence as heroic, which prepares the shock of seeing it turned against the king. When the text says “For brave Macbeth—well he deserves that name” (Act I, Scene II, line 64), it shows this directly. The Sergeant calls him "brave Macbeth" who "unseam'd" the rebel "from the nave to the chaps," and Duncan's "What he hath lost noble Macbeth hath won" echoes the witches, binding Macbeth to Cawdor's treachery.
